method: Walk zones are the Trust for Public Land's ParkServe 2025 10-minute-walk service areas (about ½ mile along the street network from each publicly accessible park). Residents come from ACS 2020–24 block groups, spread evenly over each block group's area, and are counted as served where they fall inside any walk zone; this reproduces TPL's published city figures within about 1.5 points (San Francisco 98.8% vs 99.9%, Oakland 87.2% vs 87.9%, Lancaster 19.1% vs 18.7%). The score is the average of two percentages, residents within a 10-minute walk of any park and residents within a 10-minute walk of a park of 10 acres or more, multiplied by a fairness factor: the walk-access rate in lower-income block groups (median household income under $80,000, about 80% of the state median) divided by the rate in the rest, capped at 1 when lower-income areas are at least as well served. Ranks compare the score with every other jurisdiction of the same type. Park-need priority is TPL's ranking of unserved neighborhoods within each city (very high, high, moderate); because it is relative within a city, it is not comparable across cities. ParkServe maps parks in cities and towns, so rural and unincorporated residents may be undercounted as served, and parks missing from ParkServe show as gaps.
